the stability of tree-like grids against localized intermittent power fluctuations is determined by the position of the fluctuation node in relation to the tree structure.
(i) the position of the intermittent power source is crucial for the stability of the network, (ii) the network topology plays a key role, and (iii) lossy grids are essential.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tree structure and the lossy nature of distribution grids are important factors to be considered when designing future power grids with high share of distributed resources.

the stability of a power grid against local intermittent fluctuations depends on a complex interplay of the grid's topology, its lossiness, the position of the fluctuating node and the turbulent nature of these fluctuations.
a tree-like grid with losses is more robust against intermittent fluctuations in comparison to a meshed grid with losses, but also more robust than a tree-like grid without losses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stability of synchrony in a tree-like power grid is not only determined by the position of the fluctuation source, but also depends on the coupling strength and on the topology of the grid.
a tree-like power grid is stable against localized intermittent power fluctuations if the coupling strength is high enough and losses are large enough.
tree-like distribution grids are surprisingly robust to local fluctuations, even when these are fed in at a central node.
The main takeaway from our work is that
network structure and position in the network are important to predict the influence of local intermittent fluctuations on network stability.
the stability of synchrony against localized intermittent renewable infeeds depends strongly on the network topology and the position of nodes where fluctuations are introduced into the system.
tree-like distribution grids are able to withstand local intermittent power fluctuations, but that their vulnerability is not evenly distributed.
